previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A female patient with a history of paraplegia, neurogenic bladder, and chronic abdominal pain presented with lower quadrant abdominal pain and was found to have contrast extravasation in her right forearm during a CT scan. She was admitted for monitoring of potential compartment syndrome. Over the hospital stay, her forearm edema improved, and she remained neurovascularly intact with no evidence of compartment syndrome. Abdominal pain resolved without intervention, and urine culture showed no growth, ruling out active infection. She tolerated oral intake and was managed conservatively. The patient was discharged home in stable condition with tramadol for pain, instructions to follow up with primary care, and advice to monitor for warning signs including fever, worsening pain, or urinary changes.

Brief Hospital Course:
## Urinary tract infection, with indwelling chronic foley 
catheter:  The patient was admitted for presumed complicated UTI 
despite having a UA which was only moderately positive.  The 
patient was not febrile in the hospital, and it was determined 
that her bilateral flank pain was more of a chronic issue (which 
the patient espoused) and less an indication of pyelonephritis.  
The patient had also several previous imaging studies at the end 
of ___ which was negative for anything remarkable despite the 
patient having similar complaints.  Patient was initially 
started on Bactrim, and her pain was controlled with Dilaudid 
PO.  Urine cultures were preliminarily positive for two colonies 
of gram negative rods -- as a result, the patient was discharged 
on a 10 day course of Bactrim (7 additional days as an 
outpatient), and was set up with a primary care physician at the 
___ in 1 week.

## Chronic pain syndrome:  Managed with dilaudid as needed.  
Discharged off narcotics.

types, both resistant to bactrim. A message was left for her at
